_doc: Batch m09 (medium, opus themed pass): vipers (horned, rock), vine snake, camel calf, outback dingo, two hyenas (savanna, striped), warthog, bison calf stampede, ratel pair. Motifs in motifs/medium_m09.js; every creature has its own signature motif with its own chain effect; the two hyenas share bone-snap; reptile class pieces reuse m08 venom-fang, venom-spit and tail-lash with their own palettes.

horned-viper.notes: A sand-coloured desert viper with a small horn over each eye; it shimmies sideways down into the sand until only the horns and eyes show, and warns by rubbing its saw-edged scales together in C-shaped coils.

p.u0: Horn Strike: a sand ridge runs the length of the edge with two little horns poking up, then the viper bursts out of the sand

u1.n: Sand Hide: vipers shimmy down into the sand along the edge until only their horns and eyes show, sand settling

u2.n: Rattle Warn: C-shaped coils press out of the edge and rub their saw scales, rasp ticks flying

u3.n: Buried Wait: buried vipers burst up out of the sand one after another, sand thrown off

b0.n: Horned Sandfang: sand-pale fangs launch off the edge, a venom bead at each tip, sand grains flying

b1.n: Buried Tail Whip: sandy tails whip up out of the sand and crack, dust kicked

p.b2: Horned Brow Coil: rasping C-coils line the edge in a tight guard, saw scales ticking

b3.n: Patient Burrow: vipers sink down below the edge into the sand and wait, only horns left

rock-viper.notes: A grey, rock-patterned, flat-headed mountain viper that lies among the scree like one more stone; tough-hided, it basks on hot rock and bites whatever sits on it.

p.u0: Ledge Wall: stone slabs stack along the edge into a ledge wall, a flat head sliding out of a crack

u1.n: Rock Fang: the coiled scree viper shoves out among its pebbles, flat head lifting, and drops back

u2.n: Basking Heat: hot rocks push out of the edge glowing at the base, a viper draped on each, heat rising

u3.n: Sat Upon: a flat rock is pressed down from above, cracks, and the viper under it bites up with white fangs

p.b0: Sat-On Strike: blotched vipers launch off the edge from among the pebbles

b1.n: Stony Lash: one rock-blotched viper lashes the length of the edge, pebbles kicked aside

b2.n: Ledge Camouflage: slabs line the edge in grit dust, the viper among them only a flat head in a crack

b3.n: Lichen Spray: snouts spit a fan of lichen-green venom droplets off the edge

vine-snake.notes: A vine-thin bright-green tree snake with a pointed snout and a horizontal keyhole pupil; it holds its body out stiff like a twig, sways with the leaves and leans out to strike.

p.u0: Vine Strike: one stiff vine-thin snake shoots along the length of the edge, pointed snout first
p.u1: Leaf Blend: tendrils and leaves scatter out of the edge and back, a thin snake lying along each stem, its eye showing now and then

u2.n: Whip Flick: thin bodies flick out of the edge like whips and snap back, venom drops flung off

u3.n: Early Lean: big golden keyhole eyes lock on and lean out off the edge before the strike

b0.n: Keyhole Fang: thin green rear fangs launch off the edge, a venom bead at each tip

p.b1: Creeper Whip: vine snakes lash out stiff from the edge like creepers whipping in the wind
p.b2: Leaf-Mimic Coil: vine stems and leaves line the edge, a snake coiled along each, almost invisible

b3.n: Ambush Spray: pointed snouts spit fans of green venom from the leaves

camel-calf.notes: A knobbly, fluffy desert camel calf on stilt legs it has not learned to use, with a little fluffy hump, long eyelashes against the sand, and a habit of spitting cud.

p.u0: Calf Hump Wall: fluffy hump mounds line the edge into a soft wall, fluff tufts waving

u1.n: Wobble Kick: gangly calves wobble out of the edge, one stilt leg kicking, and totter back

u2.n: Sand Fold: calves fold down and shut their long lashes against the blowing sand, then open again

u3.n: Clumsy Spit: floppy lips spit green cud blobs off the edge that splat flat

p.b0: Lanky Hoof Kick: lanky calves launch off the edge, knobbly knees splaying

b1.n: Gangly Stomp: calves stomp out of the edge on splayed stilt legs, dust puffing

p.b2: Fluff Plating: fluffy humps press together along the edge like soft plates

b3.n: Stubborn Sidestep: calves wobble off sideways out of the edge and wander back

outback-dingo.notes: A lean ginger outback dingo with pale socks, pricked ears and a white-tipped bushy tail; it lopes for miles through red dust, circles its prey, and howls instead of barking.

u0.n: Dingo Snap: ginger muzzles flash off the edge, white teeth gaping then snapping shut

u1.n: Circle Round: dingoes lope from spot to spot round the edge, paw prints left behind

u2.n: Dust Roll: dingoes roll out of the edge in red dust, paws up, and roll back

p.u3: Pale Patience: dingoes sit along the edge, muzzles raised, a long howl rising

b0.n: Dust-Pale Rake: dingoes launch off the edge in a spray of red dust

b1.n: Patient Jaw Hold: muzzles line the edge, jaws clamped shut and holding

b2.n: Dust Crouch: dingoes lie low in red dust along the edge

b3.n: Pale Shoulder Check: a dingo lopes out shoulder first and drops back

savanna-hyena.notes: A spotted grassland hyena: sloping back, big head with round ears and a dark muzzle, jaws that crack bone; it runs in a giggling pack and never forgets who wronged it.

u0.n: Cackle: grinning hyena heads hang at spots, their giggles tied together in a tripping line

u1.n: Bone Crunch: bones run the length of the edge, bend, crack and snap in two

u2.n: Scavenge: bone scraps rise off the edge, gnawed and cracked, crumbs falling

p.u3: Laugh It Off: grinning heads scatter out of the edge on a laugh and come back

b0.n: Giggle Gouge: giggling heads launch off the edge, hee marks bouncing

b1.n: Scavenger Jaw Crunch: bones shove out of the edge and snap with a crunch

b2.n: Pack Grin Stance: spotted hyenas stand shoulder to shoulder along the edge

b3.n: Pack Mob Shove: the pack lopes out of the edge together and drops back

striped-hyena.notes: A grey, black-striped desert and mountain hyena with a long mane down its back that it raises to look twice its size; a quiet scavenger that drags bones away.

u0.n: Scavenge Shove: a striped hyena shoves out of the edge, mane rising, and drops back

u1.n: Bone Drag: a bone is dragged the length of the edge, dust scuffed behind it

p.u2: Mane Bristle: long black-tipped mane hairs bristle up out of the edge

u3.n: Mane Double: striped hyenas push out of the edge and raise their manes to twice their size

b0.n: Mane Raking Swipe: mane hairs rake off the edge like claws

b1.n: Bone Crunch Jaws: bones shove out of the edge and snap

p.b2: Striped Mane Bristle: mane crests line the edge, grey and black-tipped

b3.n: Puffed-Up Shove: a hyena puffs up its mane and shoves out of the edge, dust kicked

warthog.notes: A grey grassland warthog with warts, upturned tusks and a wiry tawny mane; it trots off with its tail held straight up like an antenna and shoves through mud.

u0.n: Tusk Bash: warty faces shove out of the edge, curved tusks hooking up

u1.n: Mud Shove: snouts shove out of the edge flinging clods of mud

p.u2: Bristle Mane: wiry tawny bristles spring out of the edge with forked tips

u3.n: Tusk Lift: one warthog face runs the edge, tusks lifting under

b0.n: Tusk Hook Swipe: tusked faces launch off the edge, tusks hooking

b1.n: Tusk-Up Gore: a warthog charges the length of the edge, tusks up, tail up

b2.n: Tail-Up Stance: warthogs stand along the edge, tails straight up like flags

b3.n: Savanna Sudden Charge: a warthog bolts out of the edge, tail up, dust flying

bison-calf-stampede.notes: A stampede of rust-coloured grassland bison calves with oversized dark woolly heads and shoulder humps; they charge head-down, plant their heads, and bellow for the herd.

u0.n: Calf Charge: calves gallop out of the edge head-down and pull up

u1.n: Dust Cover: dust clouds billow out of the edge, hooves and tails kicking inside them

u2.n: Herd Bellow: calves bellow at spots, the bellow arcs tied into one tripping roar

u3.n: Heavy Lurch: one oversized woolly head lurches the length of the edge

b0.n: Hard-Head Butt: big woolly heads butt out of the edge and drop back

b1.n: Stampede Trample: dust clouds with hooves fly off the edge

p.b2: Heavy Head Plant: woolly heads plant along the edge, hooves dug in

b3.n: Herd Charge Shove: the herd shoves out of the edge in its own dust

ratel-pair.notes: A pair of grassland honey badgers, grey-white mantle over a black body, loose tough skin they can twist inside, long digging claws; fearless, tireless, they always come back for more.

p.u0: Thick Skin: ratels line the edge, twisting round inside their loose skins

u1.n: Ratel Tear: the pair shoves out of the edge together and tears back

u2.n: Rough-Up: long pale digging claws bristle out of the edge, soil flying

u3.n: Back For More: ratel pairs launch off the edge again and again, angry marks popping

b0.n: Honeyhunt Rake: digging claws rake off the edge, soil flecks flying

b1.n: Tireless Double Maul: the pair mauls out of the edge, dust kicked

b2.n: Thick Skin Shrug: ratels shrug out of the edge inside their loose skins and come back

b3.n: Honey Dig Shove: torn comb shoves out of the edge, honey dripping, bees buzzing
